questions.context: You are at a hospital. A nurse explains the rule to you.
questions.sentence: You ___ wear a mask in this ward. It is the hospital rule.
questions.explain: It is a rule, so the meaning is obligation: "must". "Might" and "could" show possibility, not a rule.

questions.context: Your friend is at the airport. The departure screen has not updated for an hour.
questions.sentence: The flight ___ be delayed. The screen has not changed.
questions.explain: You are not sure, so use "might" for a possibility. "Must be" would need strong evidence, like an official announcement.

questions.context: A shop has a sign on the door: "Closed on Sundays". You are standing outside and it is closed.
questions.sentence: Today ___ be Sunday, because the shop is closed.
questions.explain: The sign is clear evidence, so you are almost sure: "must be". "Might" would be a weak guess, which the evidence does not support.

questions.context: You are in a library. You want to photograph one page of an old book. You ask the librarian politely.
questions.sentence: Excuse me, ___ I take a photo of this page?
questions.explain: "Could I...?" is a polite way to ask permission. "Must" here would sound like an order, and "might" is not used in this way for permission.

questions.context: Your manager says the weekly report meeting is optional. You can read the notes instead.
questions.sentence: You ___ attend the meeting, but it is optional.
questions.explain: It is not necessary, so "don't have to". "Mustn't" would mean you are forbidden to attend, which is not what the manager said.

questions.context: A museum sign says: "No flash photography. This is forbidden in this room."
questions.sentence: Visitors ___ use flash in this room.
questions.explain: The sign says it is forbidden, so "mustn't". "Don't have to" and "needn't" mean it is not necessary, not that it is banned.

questions.context: Your friend has had a cough for two weeks and keeps smoking. You want to help.
questions.sentence: You ___ see a doctor about that cough.
questions.explain: This is friendly advice, so "should". "Must" would sound too forceful, and "might" is only a guess.

questions.context: You forgot your friend's birthday. Now you feel bad about it.
questions.sentence: I ___ remembered your birthday. I feel terrible.
questions.explain: You are talking about a regret in the past, so "should have + past participle". "Must have" would be a conclusion, not regret.

questions.context: Your phone is missing. The only place you have been without it is a taxi, and you remember leaving it on the seat.
questions.sentence: You ___ left it in the taxi. That is the only place you have been without it.
questions.explain: The evidence is strong, so you are almost sure about the past: "must have". "Might have" is weaker, and "can't have" would mean it is impossible.

questions.context: Your friend says he saw you at the cinema at 7 pm. But you were at home all evening.
questions.sentence: I ___ been at the cinema. I was at home all evening.
questions.explain: It was impossible in the past, so "couldn't have + past participle". "Mustn't have" would mean you were not allowed to go.

questions.context: You are in a busy café and want the waiter to bring the bill. You speak politely.
questions.sentence: Excuse me, ___ bring the bill, please?
questions.explain: "Could you" is the most polite request. "Must you" sounds demanding, and "Can't you" sounds annoyed.

questions.context: When you were ten, you swam across the river every summer. Your friend asks about it.
questions.sentence: When I was ten, I ___ swim across the river.
questions.explain: This is past ability, so "could". "Can" is for the present, and "must" and "should" are not about ability.

questions.context: You have two ways to get home. A taxi costs a lot of money. The walk takes 40 minutes, but you do not mind.
questions.sentence: Honestly, I ___ walk than pay for a taxi.
questions.explain: You are stating a preference between two options, so "would rather ... than". The other modals do not express preference.

questions.context: Your teacher tells the class that the test results are ready and will come out on Monday.
questions.sentence: The results ___ be ready by Monday. That is what the office said.
questions.explain: "Should" describes what is expected to happen according to a plan. "Might" would mean it is only possible, and "must" would sound like a rule.

sections.heading: What is a modal verb?
text: Modal verbs are helper verbs. They add meaning to the main verb: ability, permission, obligation, advice, or how sure you are. The common ones are can, could, may, might, must, should, will and would.
Modal verbs never change for the subject. Say "she can swim", not "she cans swim".

sections.heading: Grammar pattern
text: Modal + base verb, with no "to": "You should leave now", not "You should to leave".
Negative: add "not" after the modal. "You must not park here" or "You mustn't park here".
Question: swap the subject and the modal. "Can I sit here?" "Should we wait?"

sections.heading: Ability and permission
text: Can and could show ability: "I can swim." "When I was ten, I could swim across the river."
For permission, "may" is formal and "can" or "could" is common in speech: "May I come in?" "Could I ask a question?"

sections.heading: Obligation, and no obligation
text: "Must" and "have to" both show that something is required. "Must" often comes from the speaker's own rule or feeling. "Have to" often comes from outside, like a law, a school or a boss.
"Don't have to" means it is not necessary. "Mustn't" means it is forbidden. These two are different: "You don't have to pay" is fine, but "You mustn't pay" means you are not allowed to.

sections.heading: Advice and expectation
text: "Should" and "ought to" give advice or say what is expected: "You should rest." "The package should arrive on Monday."
"Must" is stronger and sounds like a rule. Use it carefully, because it can sound too forceful in advice.

sections.heading: Deduction: how sure are you?
text: "It must be true" means you are almost sure, based on clear evidence. "It might be true" means it is possible. "It can't be true" means you are sure it is not.
Look at the evidence in the situation. Clear proof points to "must". A weak guess points to "might".

sections.heading: Past forms
text: "Should have + past participle" shows regret: "I should have called you."
"Must have + past participle" is a strong conclusion about the past: "She must have missed the bus."
"Couldn't have + past participle" means it was impossible: "I couldn't have been at the cinema; I was at home."

sections.heading: Polite requests
text: "Could you...?" and "Would you mind...?" are more polite than "Can you...?". "Must you...?" sounds rude or demanding.
